description: Somos un equipo de 5 estudiantes de ingeniería en software de México que cree que aprender ingeniería espacial no tiene por qué ser aburrido, aunque nuestro nombre diga lo contrario. Estamos haciendo un juego web cooperativo en pixel art donde de 1 a 4 jugadores dirigen una agencia espacial
summary:
Go/No Go is an online multiplayer web game where 1 to 4 players run a space agency together. Each player takes a role: Engineering, Science, Telecommunications, or Mission Control. The team accepts missions and designs a satellite by choosing its structure, power, instruments, communications, orbit, and launch vehicle, all within limits on mass, energy, budget, and time. They then work through the mission phases by completing minigames in a shared 2D office. The live launch succeeds or fails based on their design choices and how well they coordinated. A final report breaks down every percentage and explains the outcome.

The Space Mission Design Game challenge points out that students rarely get to try designing a full mission, so the trade-offs between science, engineering, and resources stay abstract. Go/No Go turns those trade-offs into concrete decisions with visible consequences. Its name comes from the “Go/No Go” poll held before a real launch, where every team must give its approval. The game shows that space missions depend on teamwork and informed decisions, and its data is fact-checked against NASA sources.
details:
Go/No Go runs in the browser from a link, with nothing to install. One player creates a room and shares a four-character code, and up to three teammates join. Each player picks a role: Engineering, Science, Telecommunications, or Mission Control.

A mission has these stages:

  1. Management: The agency has funds, time, and reputation, and pays monthly salaries. The team decides which missions and partnerships to accept.
  2. Design: Players build a satellite from real component types, such as 1U, 3U, or 6U CubeSats, solar panels, cameras, radios, and attitude control. They must stay within mass, volume, power, budget, and schedule limits. Each component comes in a flight-proven “heritage” version or a cheaper “new” version that carries more risk. Players also choose a launch option: an educational ride from the ISS, a shared rideshare to sun-synchronous orbit, or a dedicated launch.
  3. Execution: Each phase has tasks, played as minigames in a shared top-down 2D office: assembly, instrument calibration, radio tuning, and vibration and thermal-vacuum testing. Anyone can do any task, but the right role does it better. Random events, such as a launch delay, force the team to adapt.
  4. Launch and report: The launch plays out live as a series of stages, and each stage’s success chance comes from the team’s choices. A final report breaks down every percentage and explains why the mission turned out as it did.

The playable demo is a tutorial mission that ends with the agency’s first CubeSat in orbit.

Benefits and expected impact

  • Students get hands-on experience with real mission trade-offs, which are usually only taught in theory.
  • The game teaches teamwork, communication, and shared decision-making, which matter as much as technical knowledge in real space programs.
  • The report turns failure into feedback: players learn why something went wrong, not just that it did.
  • The game runs in any browser and in both Spanish and English, so it fits classrooms with few resources.
  • The long-term vision is for the agency to grow from CubeSats all the way to starting a colony on Mars.

Tools and technology

  • Languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with native ES modules, no frameworks, and no build step for the game client. The main menu prototype uses Vite.
  • Multiplayer: Each room runs on a Cloudflare Durable Object, which acts as the authority. It runs the same game-state code as the client.
  • Hosting: Cloudflare Pages publishes the game as a static site that updates with every merge.
  • Data: A JSON catalog holds components, orbits, launch vehicles, tasks, and missions. Each value is linked to its source, and a script validates the catalog.
  • Design: Figma and FigJam for brainstorming, wireframes, pixel art, and the style guide.
  • Collaboration: GitHub for version control, issues, and the hackathon plan.
  • Hardware: None needed. A computer with a web browser is enough.

Creativity

  • The name and the core tension come from the real “Go/No Go” poll held before every launch.
  • The pixel-art style, called “Agencia 1975”, has a retro space-agency look: cream paper, navy ink, and mission red. One proposal uses animals that flew to space as the player characters.
  • The launch success percentages come from the players’ own decisions and coordination, so every launch feels earned and tense.
  • An in-game wiki explains the concepts and cites its sources.

What the team considered

  • Accuracy: Data is fact-checked against NASA and other agencies’ sources.
  • Accessibility: There are options for larger text, reduced motion, and sound. Room codes leave out characters that are easy to confuse, like 0/O and 1/I/L.
  • Inclusion: The game is bilingual (Spanish and English) and needs no installation.
  • Scope: Every feature must trace back to a requirement of the challenge, which keeps the project focused for the hackathon.
  • Teamwork: The work was divided by area: game design and engine, menu and fact-checking, art and UI/UX, scientific interfaces, and minigame layout. The design document is the single source of truth
